title: Cosmology I: geometry and kinematics of an expanding universe
scope: The geometry of a homogeneous, isotropic universe and what observers measure in it, independent of which matter drives the expansion. Covers the cosmological and Copernican principles, homogeneity and isotropy, comoving observers, Weyl's postulate and cosmic time; the FLRW metric, its curvature, the parameter k and the three spatial geometries with their topology; the scale factor, Hubble parameter, Hubble-Lemaitre law, peculiar velocity and the non-expansion of bound systems; light propagation, cosmological redshift and energy non-conservation; proper, comoving, luminosity and angular-diameter distances, the Hubble radius, lookback time, the deceleration parameter and cosmography; conformal time, particle and event horizons, and Penrose diagrams of FLRW models. How the field equations fix a(t), specific model universes and measured parameters belong to cosmological-dynamics and physical-cosmology.

concepts.title: Cosmology
concepts.summary: Cosmology treats the whole Universe as a single physical system, asking about its large-scale geometry, contents and history. In general relativity this means finding a spacetime metric that solves the field equations for the smoothed-out matter and energy of the Universe.
concepts.notes: Include the argument for why cosmology needs GR at all: at fixed density the compactness M/R grows as R^2, so it reaches order unity at a few Gpc, inside the observable Universe (Schutz ch13). Also note the uniqueness of the system: no repeatable experiments.

concepts.title: Spatial homogeneity
concepts.summary: A spatial slice is homogeneous when every point on it is equivalent to every other: some isometry of the slice carries any point to any other, so on large scales the density and statistical properties of the Universe are the same everywhere at a given cosmic time.
concepts.notes: Observational care: deep observations look back in time, so homogeneity is a statement about constant-time slices, not about what we see on the sky.

concepts.title: Spatial isotropy
concepts.summary: Isotropy about a point means no spatial direction there is preferred: an isometry fixing the point can rotate any direction into any other. A space isotropic about every point is automatically homogeneous, but a homogeneous space need not be isotropic (think of a uniform field pointing one way).

concepts.title: Copernican principle
concepts.summary: The Copernican principle is the working assumption that we occupy no special place in the Universe, so observers elsewhere at the same epoch would see essentially the same cosmos. It is the conceptual ancestor of the cosmological principle and implies the expansion is not centred on us.

concepts.title: Cosmological principle
concepts.summary: The cosmological principle asserts that, once structure below roughly 100 Mpc is averaged out, the Universe is spatially homogeneous and isotropic at each cosmic time. Geometrically, spacetime is sliced into spacelike hypersurfaces each homogeneous and isotropic about all its points, which is extremely restrictive on the metric.
concepts.notes: Schutz motivates it with observers whose past light cones never overlapped yet see alike regions; DIV supports it with CMB isotropy and contrasts it with Charlier's hierarchical cosmology, an unending hierarchy of clusters with no smooth average density.

concepts.title: Homogeneity scale and coarse-graining
concepts.summary: Cosmological models treat matter as a smooth fluid obtained by averaging galaxies over regions of about 100 Mpc or more, above which the averaged density is uniform. The models make no claim about structure on smaller scales.

concepts.title: Perfect cosmological principle
concepts.summary: The perfect cosmological principle strengthens the cosmological principle by requiring the large-scale Universe to look the same at every time as well as every place. It was the founding assumption of steady-state theory and geometrically leads to de Sitter spacetime.

concepts.title: Comoving observer
concepts.summary: A comoving (fundamental) observer moves with the smoothed cosmic fluid, the substratum whose particles are averaged galaxies. Only such observers see the Universe as isotropic; their world lines are timelike geodesics and their proper time is cosmic time.
concepts.notes: GA ch33 invokes comoving observers only as motivation for the Lie derivative along a fluid flow.

concepts.title: Weyl's postulate
concepts.summary: Weyl's postulate states that the world lines of the cosmic substratum form a smooth congruence of timelike geodesics that never cross, except possibly at an initial or final singularity. It guarantees a single well-defined matter four-velocity at every event.

concepts.title: Local cosmological rest frame
concepts.summary: At each event the local cosmological rest frame is the local inertial frame in which the cosmic microwave background shows no dipole anisotropy. It moves with the Hubble flow and is a cleaner definition than the average motion of nearby galaxies, which have bulk flows.

concepts.title: Orthogonality of comoving world lines to homogeneous slices
concepts.summary: In a homogeneous, isotropic cosmology the comoving world lines must meet the homogeneous slices at right angles, because any tilt would single out a spatial direction. In comoving coordinates this gives g_0i = 0, and with t as proper time g_00 = -1.

names: orthogonality of world lines to homogeneous slices

merged_from: orthogonality of world lines to homogeneous slices

concepts.title: Cosmic time
concepts.summary: Cosmic time is a global time coordinate whose constant-time slices are the homogeneous, isotropic hypersurfaces and which equals the proper time of comoving observers. It defines a cosmic simultaneity reflecting the matter distribution, not a violation of relativity, and can be read off any uniformly evolving quantity such as the CMB temperature.

concepts.title: Comoving coordinates
concepts.summary: Comoving coordinates label each comoving observer by fixed spatial coordinates and use cosmic time as the time coordinate. All expansion then lives in the time dependence of the spatial metric, and physical separations equal the scale factor times fixed comoving separations.
concepts.notes: Physical (proper) separations at fixed cosmic time are a(t) times comoving ones (GA ch15 pairs the two).

concepts.title: World map and world picture
concepts.summary: The world map is the Universe on one slice of constant cosmic time, everything 'as it is now', which no one can observe. The world picture is what an observer actually sees, lying on their past light cone, so more distant objects appear as they were at earlier cosmic times.

concepts.title: Scale factor
concepts.summary: The scale factor a(t) is the single function of cosmic time multiplying the spatial metric, so every proper distance between comoving points grows by the same ratio a(t2)/a(t1). It is usually normalized to 1 today; growth that differed between directions would violate isotropy.
concepts.notes: A comoving volume scales as a^3 (GA ch50). Books differ on whether a is dimensionless (normalized today) or carries length (GA ch16, DIV for k = +/-1, where it is the radius of the 3-sphere).

concepts.title: Hubble parameter
concepts.summary: The Hubble parameter H = (da/dt)/a is the fractional expansion rate; its present value H0, the Hubble constant, is about 70 km/s/Mpc. It generally changes with time, and 1/H0 sets the characteristic Hubble time of the Universe.
concepts.notes: The Hubble constant (H0 as present value, units km/s/Mpc) is folded here; measuring it, the h convention and the Hubble tension belong to physical-cosmology.

concepts.title: Hubble-Lemaitre law
concepts.summary: On average galaxies recede with speed proportional to distance, v = H0 d. Uniform scaling of all distances is the only velocity field that keeps a homogeneous Universe homogeneous, so every comoving observer sees the same law; the recession due purely to growth of a(t) is called the Hubble flow.

names: v = H d from any galaxy

concepts.notes: Observationally it is a low-redshift relation z ~ H0 d; exactly, in any FLRW model the proper distance to a comoving galaxy obeys d(dp)/dt = H dp at all distances. Renamed by the IAU in 2018.

concepts.title: Peculiar velocity
aliases: motion relative to the Hubble flow
concepts.summary: A peculiar velocity is a galaxy's motion relative to the local comoving frame, caused by local gravitational pulls and superposed on the Hubble flow. It is small (below about 1e-3 c) but dominates the redshifts of very nearby galaxies, and a freely moving particle's peculiar momentum decays as 1/a with expansion.

names: decay of peculiar momentum with expansion

merged_from: decay of peculiar momentum with expansion
concepts.notes: GA Exercise 15.6 shows the decay of peculiar momentum with radial geodesics in de Sitter; this is the massive-particle counterpart of cosmological redshift.

concepts.title: Bound systems do not expand
concepts.summary: Atoms, planetary systems, stars and galaxies are held together by local forces and are not stretched by the cosmic scale factor; the expanding FLRW description applies only above the homogeneity scale. A common misconception is that space expands everywhere, dragging bound objects apart.

names: why bound systems do not expand

concepts.title: Three-sphere
concepts.summary: The three-sphere is the set of points at fixed distance a from the origin of four-dimensional Euclidean space, with metric a^2[dchi^2 + sin^2 chi dOmega^2]. It is compact with no boundary and finite volume 2 pi^2 a^3, and spheres drawn around any point first grow then shrink to zero area at chi = pi.

concepts.title: Hyperbolic 3-space
concepts.summary: Hyperbolic 3-space is the space of constant negative curvature, with metric a^2[dchi^2 + sinh^2 chi dOmega^2] and infinite volume. It can be embedded as a hyperboloid in four-dimensional Minkowski space but not in Euclidean space.

concepts.title: Robertson-Walker metric
concepts.summary: The Robertson-Walker (FLRW) metric ds^2 = -dt^2 + a(t)^2[dr^2/(1-kr^2) + r^2 dOmega^2] is the most general spacetime whose constant-time slices are homogeneous and isotropic. The scale factor a(t) carries all the dynamics and k = +1, 0, -1 fixes the spatial geometry; the matter content only enters later through the field equations.

names: homogeneity from a constant curvature scalar
three-dimensional Riemann tensor of spatial slices

merged_from: homogeneity from a constant curvature scalar
three-dimensional Riemann tensor of spatial slices
concepts.notes: Derivation routes differ: Schutz demands a constant curvature scalar on an isotropic 3-metric (homogeneity from a constant curvature scalar); GA and DIV quote the constant-curvature 3-metric; GA ch16 argues that homogeneity and isotropy leave the spatial Riemann tensor K(gamma_ik gamma_jl - gamma_il gamma_jk), with spatial Ricci scalar 6K (not the spacetime quantities). The hyperspherical form with dchi = dr/sqrt(1-kr^2), r = sin chi, chi, sinh chi (GA ch16 boxed summary) is the most useful for light propagation. DIV uses signature (+,-,-,-). Every FLRW spacetime is conformally flat. Robertson and Walker proved generality in 1935.

concepts.title: Curvature index k
concepts.summary: The constant k in the FLRW metric gives the sign of spatial curvature: +1 for spherical (closed) slices, 0 for flat, -1 for hyperbolic (open). Rescaling r and a can set its magnitude to 1 but never change its sign, and the physical curvature of a slice is k/a^2.

names: coordinate slicings of de Sitter spacetime

merged_from: coordinate slicings of de Sitter spacetime
concepts.notes: Confusion to address: k describes space, not spacetime, and depends on how spacetime is sliced; de Sitter can be written with k = +1, 0 or -1 (GA Exercises 18.6-18.7). The link between k and density relative to critical (Omega - 1) belongs to cosmological-dynamics; with Lambda nonzero, geometry no longer decides recollapse.

concepts.title: Spatially flat universe
concepts.summary: In the k = 0 case each constant-time slice is ordinary Euclidean 3-space scaled by a(t), infinite in extent. Its spacetime is still curved whenever a(t) is not constant, since the Riemann tensor involves the expansion rate and acceleration.
concepts.notes: Legacy misconception check: 'k = 0 FLRW is flat spacetime' is wrong. GA ch36 computes its curvature by Cartan's method as a first time-dependent example.

concepts.title: Closed universe
concepts.summary: In the k = +1 case each spatial slice is a three-sphere of radius a(t): finite volume 2 pi^2 a^3, no edge and no centre, with circles whose circumference is less than 2 pi times their radius. Light can travel around the Universe, so a source may in principle appear in more than one direction.
concepts.notes: The balloon analogy fits this case best, but the extra embedding dimension is only a visual aid. GA Example 19.10 follows ghost images of a source seen the short and long way around on the k = +1 Penrose diagram. Whether a closed universe recollapses is a dynamical question (cosmological-dynamics).

concepts.title: Open hyperbolic universe
concepts.summary: In the k = -1 case each spatial slice is hyperbolic 3-space of curvature -1/a^2: infinite volume, diverging parallel geodesics, triangle angles summing to less than pi, and circles with circumference exceeding 2 pi times their radius.
concepts.notes: Schutz proves homogeneity by recognizing the slice as the hyperboloid of fixed timelike interval in Minkowski spacetime, whose Lorentz boosts move any point to any other. The k = +1 slice embeds as a sphere in Euclidean R^4, but the whole k = -1 slice needs a Minkowski ambient space (GA ch16 embedding of spatial sections). GA uses the Poincare disc and Lambert triangle formula to build intuition.

concepts.title: Cosmic topology
concepts.summary: Local curvature does not fix the global shape of space: the simplest choices are S^3 for k = +1 and R^3 for k = 0 or -1, but identifying points can make flat or hyperbolic slices finite with the same local geometry.

concepts.title: Curvature of the FLRW metric
concepts.summary: The FLRW metric has connection coefficients such as Gamma^i_tj = (da/dt / a) delta^i_j, and in an orthonormal frame R_tt = -3 a"/a with Ricci scalar R = 6(a"/a + (da/dt)^2/a^2 + k/a^2). These components are the geometric input that turns the field equations into the Friedmann equations.

concepts.notes: For k = 0 the orthonormal Riemann components are a"/a (time-space) and (da/dt / a)^2 (space-space). FLRW has vanishing Weyl tensor. Radiation-dominated FLRW has R = 0 but is not flat (legacy capstone).

concepts.title: Proper distance in cosmology
concepts.summary: The proper distance to a comoving object is the length measured along a slice of constant cosmic time, l(t) = a(t) chi. It grows with the scale factor but cannot be measured directly, because we only receive light from the past.

names: proper distance in a Robertson–Walker spacetime

merged_from: proper distance in a Robertson–Walker spacetime

concepts.title: Recession velocity
concepts.summary: The recession velocity is the rate of change of proper distance with cosmic time, v = H d. It exceeds the speed of light beyond the Hubble radius without contradicting relativity, because it is not a velocity measured by any local observer.
concepts.notes: Schutz raises the objection that v = H d exceeds c beyond about 4200 Mpc, answered by the locality of the velocity concept.

concepts.title: Hubble radius
concepts.summary: The Hubble radius c/H is the proper distance at which the recession velocity equals the speed of light. It is an expansion scale, not in general a causal horizon, and should not be confused with the particle or event horizon.
concepts.notes: No book candidate names it; added from the legacy three-horizon table (flat dust: particle horizon 3ct, Hubble radius 1.5ct, no event horizon).

concepts.title: Radial light rays in FLRW spacetime
aliases: radial null geodesic in a Robertson-Walker spacetime
narrowing of light cones in comoving coordinates
concepts.summary: A radial light ray in FLRW obeys dt = a(t) dchi, so the comoving distance it covers is the integral of dt/a. Drawn in comoving coordinates and cosmic time, light cones narrow as the Universe expands, since light crosses less comoving distance per unit time.

names: narrowing of light cones in comoving coordinates
radial null geodesic in a Robertson–Walker spacetime
radial light rays in Robertson-Walker spacetime

merged_from: radial null geodesic in a Robertson–Walker spacetime
radial light rays in Robertson-Walker spacetime
narrowing of light cones in comoving coordinates
concepts.notes: GA Exercise 24.4 treats chi as cyclic so a^2 u^chi is conserved along the ray.

concepts.title: Comoving distance
concepts.summary: The comoving distance to a source is the fixed coordinate separation chi = integral of dt/a along the light ray from emission to reception (times a0 if a carries length). The source radial coordinate is r = sin chi, chi or sinh chi for k = +1, 0, -1, and multiplying by a(t) gives proper distance at time t.
concepts.notes: Legacy distinguishes comoving radial distance D_C from transverse comoving distance D_M = a0 S_k(D_C/a0).

concepts.title: Conformal time
concepts.summary: Conformal time tau is defined by dtau = dt/a(t), which turns the FLRW metric into a(tau)^2 times a static metric. Radial light rays then move at 45 degrees in (tau, chi), and the conformal time elapsed equals the comoving distance light has covered.

concepts.title: Cosmological redshift
aliases: wavelength stretching with the scale factor
concepts.summary: Light travelling between comoving observers has its wavelength stretched in proportion to the scale factor, 1 + z = a(t_obs)/a(t_em). It is a blueshift in a contracting universe, reduces to an ordinary Doppler shift z = v for nearby sources, and is distinct from both kinematic Doppler and static gravitational redshift.

names: redshift as a cosmological distance label
Doppler versus gravitational versus cosmological redshift
wavelength stretching with the scale factor

merged_from: wavelength stretching with the scale factor
Doppler versus gravitational versus cosmological redshift
redshift as a cosmological distance label
concepts.notes: Derivations: two successive crests covering the same comoving interval (GA, DIV); conserved covariant momentum p_chi so observed energy scales as 1/a (Schutz Ex. 13.9); conformal invariance of electromagnetism (GA Ex. 19.5). The stretching also applies to neutrinos and gravitational waves. Because z grows monotonically with distance, astronomers use it as a label for distance and epoch.

concepts.title: Energy conservation in an expanding universe
aliases: non-conservation of photon energy in cosmology
concepts.summary: A time-dependent FLRW metric has no timelike Killing vector, so there is no conserved total energy along a photon path and the energy lost to cosmological redshift is not transferred anywhere. Local energy-momentum conservation still holds; the global law simply does not exist in such a spacetime.

names: non-conservation of photon energy in cosmology

merged_from: non-conservation of photon energy in cosmology

concepts.title: Redshift drift
concepts.summary: The redshift of a given comoving source changes slowly as the observer's time advances, according to dz/dt_obs = (1+z)H(t_obs) - H(t_em). Measuring it would track the expansion history directly rather than through distance measures.

concepts.title: Lookback time
concepts.summary: Because light travels at finite speed, a more distant source is seen as it was at an earlier cosmic time; the lookback time is the cosmic time elapsed between emission of light received with redshift z and its reception. For small z it is approximately [z - (1 + q0/2) z^2]/H0.
concepts.notes: The exact emission time t(z) requires the Friedmann equation (cosmological-dynamics).

concepts.title: Deceleration parameter
concepts.summary: The deceleration parameter q = -a a"/(da/dt)^2 is the dimensionless measure of whether cosmic expansion is slowing (q > 0) or speeding up (q < 0). Named when gravity was expected to decelerate expansion, it is negative for today's accelerating Universe, with q0 roughly -0.55.
concepts.notes: Its relation to density parameters, q0 = Omega_m/2 - Omega_Lambda for matter plus Lambda, requires the Friedmann equations. Model values: 1/2 Einstein-de Sitter, -1 steady state or de Sitter.

concepts.title: Cosmography
concepts.summary: Cosmography maps the expansion history, a(t) or H(z), through distance measures and redshifts without yet using Einstein's equations. It expands the scale factor in a Taylor series about today, so H0 and q0 appear as the first coefficients.

concepts.title: Luminosity distance
concepts.summary: The luminosity distance d_L = sqrt(L/4 pi F) is the distance at which a source of known luminosity would give the observed flux in static Euclidean space. In FLRW, d_L = a0 r (1+z), larger than the present transverse distance by a factor 1+z because each photon loses energy and photons arrive stretched out in time.
concepts.notes: Convention trap: DIV defines d_L with the redshift losses divided out, so its d_L = r1 R(t0) lacks the (1+z) factor of the standard (Schutz, legacy) definition. It is what standard candles and standard sirens measure.

concepts.title: Angular-diameter distance
concepts.summary: The angular-diameter distance d_A = D/theta is the distance at which an object of known proper size D would subtend the observed angle in Euclidean space. In FLRW, d_A = a(t_em) r = d_L/(1+z)^2, and it can decrease with redshift beyond z of order 1, so very distant objects look larger.
concepts.notes: The reciprocity d_L = (1+z)^2 d_A (Etherington distance duality) holds for any metric theory with photon conservation. Key uses are the CMB acoustic scale and baryon acoustic oscillations as standard rulers (physical-cosmology).

concepts.title: Second-order Hubble law
concepts.summary: Expanding the scale factor to second order about today gives H0 d_L = z + (1 - q0) z^2/2 + ..., so departures from the linear Hubble law at moderate redshift measure the deceleration parameter.

names: luminosity distance to second order in z

concepts.notes: DIV's form d_L = z T0[1 - (1+q0)z/2] uses its own d_L convention (differs by 1+z). The magnitude-redshift (Hubble) diagram is its observational form (physical-cosmology).

concepts.title: Exact luminosity distance-redshift relation
concepts.summary: For a given model the exact d_L(z) follows by writing the comoving distance as an integral over the Friedmann expansion rate, d_L = (1+z) a0 S_k(chi) with chi an integral of dz/H(z). Fitting it to distant supernovae constrains a combination of the matter and dark-energy density parameters.
concepts.notes: DIV's version uses its d_L convention and an effective potential for the scale factor. The steady-state (de Sitter) case gives d_L exactly proportional to z (a cosmological-dynamics candidate).

concepts.title: Particle horizon
concepts.summary: The particle horizon separates the comoving particles an observer could have seen since the Big Bang from those whose light has not yet arrived. Its present proper distance is a(t) times the integral of dt'/a from 0 to t (3ct for matter domination), it grows with time, and it exists only when the past boundary of spacetime is spacelike.
concepts.notes: Equals 2ct for radiation domination; under exponential expansion it grows like exp(Ht)/H. This is the root of the horizon problem (physical-cosmology).

concepts.title: Cosmological event horizon
concepts.summary: An observer's cosmological event horizon bounds the events from which signals can ever reach them: it is the past light cone of the observer's endpoint at future infinity. It exists when the comoving distance light can travel in the infinite future is finite, as in eternally accelerating universes like de Sitter, and sources crossing it redshift toward infinity.

names: reception time divergence at the horizon

merged_from: reception time divergence at the horizon
concepts.notes: Misconception: a galaxy crossing our horizon does not vanish at an observable moment; its signals arrive ever later and more redshifted (z and d_L diverge) while it crosses in finite proper time, where its recession speed reaches c (DIV ch25). GA ch19 pairs it with the past event horizon, the future light cone of the observer's starting point on past infinity, bounding what the observer can ever influence; seeing and influencing are separate questions. GA also applies that name to flat and open dust models, where most texts speak only of particle horizons. In de Sitter with a comoving observer at r = 0, the horizon sits at proper distance c/H. Flat dust has no event horizon.

concepts.title: Penrose diagram of FLRW spacetime
concepts.summary: Using conformal time, each FLRW model maps onto part of the Einstein static cylinder and compactifies to a two-dimensional causal diagram. The Big Bang appears as a spacelike boundary: a triangle for k = 0 or -1 dust and a rectangle with spacelike bang and crunch for k = +1, which shows at a glance why particle horizons exist.

names: big bang singularity as a spacelike boundary

merged_from: big bang singularity as a spacelike boundary
concepts.notes: Spacelike initial singularity: different comoving observers start from causally disconnected points of it. The de Sitter square diagram and the inextendibility of matter-filled FLRW models are handled in cosmological-dynamics and causal-structure-and-singularities.
